1178.dq: A phonological word can only carry one primary stress. ... A phonological word in Ibaloy can only have one primary stress which is either penultimate or final.
1178.dloc: Ch.1 §1.2 Stress, §1.2.1 Root Stress, §1.2.2 Exceptions (pp.12-15); Ch.6 §6.1 Stress-Shift (pp.63-64); abstract
1178.heavy: No stress-ATTRACTING heavy class is stated. The conditioning is on the root-initial syllable only: a closed (CVC) sigma1 or a sigma1 containing the central vowel /ə/ is SKIPPED (stress goes to sigma2); an open sigma1 with a full vowel (i, a, o) is stressed. I.e. closed syllables repel rather than attract initial stress, and schwa behaves as an unstressable/reduced vowel. No vowel-length contrast.
1178.dflt: When sigma1 is open with a full vowel: stress sigma1, then every second syllable; primary = rightmost, i.e. 2-syll penult, 3-syll final, (4-syll penult by the stated alternation). Monosyllables stressed.
1178.prule: Word-level; one primary stress per phonological word, always penultimate or final. Root stress predictable from the root-initial syllable: if sigma1 is open and its vowel is not /ə/ (central vowel; the repository renders it '/a/' or '/8/', the page has /ə/), sigma1 is stressed; if sigma1 is closed (CVC) or contains /ə/, sigma2 is stressed; then every second syllable rightward is stressed; the rightmost stress is primary, others secondary. Hence 2-syll CV.CV(C) = penult ('mata 'eye'), CVC.CV(C) or Cə.CV(C) = final (tak'laj 'hand', sə'li 'foot'); 3-syll CV.CV.CV = final with secondary on sigma1 (ˌʔasə'wa 'spouse', ˌʔada'wi 'far'), CVC/Cə-initial 3-syll = penult (kə'jakan 'armpit', siʔ'gada '3+/IND'). Monosyllables stressed.
1178.srule: Roots (the only domain the author analyses for secondary stress): every second syllable rightward from the first stressed syllable (sigma1 if open with a non-/ə/ vowel, else sigma2) is stressed; the rightmost stress is primary and all others secondary — so CV-initial trisyllabic roots carry an initial secondary stress (ˌʔasə'wa [ˌʔasəb'bʷa] 'spouse', ˌʔada'wi 'far'), while disyllabic and CVC/Cə-initial trisyllabic roots have none. Outside roots secondary stress ('phonological and pragmatic conditioning') is left unanalysed; stress-shift prefixes/infixes carry inherent secondary stress (/ˌmanlo'to/ [ˌmando'to]).

1179.dq: O acento pode ser definido como o troquéu moraico. Quando a palavra é formada de apensas sílabas leves, a sílaba à esquerda recebe o acento, já quando há uma sílaba pesada, devido ao alongamento da vogal, esta sílaba será acentuada. (also: 'A palavra mínina em idaté é constituída prosodicamente de no mínimo duas moras, pois os monossílabos tônicos sempre são alongados'; secondary vs primary stres…
1179.dloc: Cap. 6 'Acento', pp. 114-119 (cited passage pp. 114-116; the TOC lists the chapter at 113); also Cap. 5 p. 106 (coda non-moraic, ex. 115 [ˈu.ɾus]), §4.3 pp. 99-100 (vogais alongadas), Conclusão p. 120
1179.heavy: Heavy = bimoraic rhyme via a long (lengthened) vowel, CVː or CVːC; 'a coda não contribui para o peso silábico em idaté' (CVC with short V is light, e.g. [ˈu.ɾus], [ˈmɔ.len]).
1179.prule: Moraic trochee at the right edge (author's analysis after Hayes 1995): words of light syllables only take penultimate stress ([ˈwa.ɾi], [ma.ˈla.ɦo], [ˈmɔ.len], [ˈu.ɾus]; codas are not moraic); a heavy syllable = one with a lengthened vowel (CVː or CVːC) attracts stress, and such syllables are word-final, giving final stress ([laˈbaːs], [maˈʔeːs], [ba.ˈɾiː]), which the author calls 'excepcional'. Monosyllables lengthen to meet a bimoraic word minimum ([aː], [lɔː]).
1179.srule: Only in compounds: in two-member compounds each member keeps its penultimate stress, the last member's stress being primary and the first member's secondary ((ˌma.nu)(ˈa.man) 'galo', (ˌbataɾ)(ˈsenaɾ) 'pipoca'): 'O acento secundário é permitido em idaté, e podemos observá-lo nas palavras compostas... a última receberá o acento primário e a primeira o secundário'. No secondary or rhythmic stress is described within simplex words (none longer than three syllables exemplified).

1183.tone: Doke §29 (p. 144-145): three level tones (high, mid, low), gliding tones only in onomatopoeia; 'There are numerous cases, in which tone is significant in Ila' (minimal pairs e.g. cita 'do' vs cita 'I don't know', inanda 'house' vs 'forked pole'); 'the tones are practically levelled out in sentences'. Doke explicitly separates tone from stress: raised tone on an initial or final syllable 'gives an impression of stress' but that syllable 'is not stressed'. A dedicated tonal study exists (Yukawa 1987, 'A tonological study of Ila verbs', ILCAA Studies in Zambian Languages, pp. 185-256; open copy in the TUFS repository, record 11526); it analyses verbal tone and says nothing about stress placement. Ila is thus a tone language WITH a stated (hedged) penultimate stress default; coded fixed and quantity-insensitive on the stress statement, tone recorded here.

tn.quote: 3.2.1. Для сойкинского диалекта ижорского языка предлагается система из двух акцентов: легкого /'/ и тяжелого / `/. … Квантитативные оппозиции сегментов в рамках стопы являются важнейшим фонетическим признаком, противопоставляющим акценты в ижорском, но, возможно, не единственным. В отличие от падающего тонального контура на стопе, характерного для нейтральной реализации легкого акцента, в стопах, маркированных тяжелым акцентом, отмечено некоторое повышение тона к концу продленного гласного 2-го слога. Однако оно зафиксировано на очень ограниченном материале …
tn.translation: 3.2.1. For the Soikkola dialect of Ingrian a system of two accents is proposed: light /'/ and heavy /`/. … Quantitative oppositions of segments within the foot are the most important phonetic feature distinguishing the accents in Ingrian, but possibly not the only one. Unlike the falling tonal contour on the foot that is characteristic of the neutral realisation of the light accent, in feet marked by the heavy accent some rise of pitch towards the end of the lengthened 2nd-syllable vowel has been noted. However, it was recorded on very limited material …

tn.note: No lexical tone. Word prosody has two lexicalised foot 'accents' (light vs heavy) cued by segmental quantity, not pitch; each foot has a falling pitch contour with the stressed first syllable higher.

1193.dq: The domain of the lexical tone is the nominal stem; noun class prefixes are toneless.
1193.dloc: Section 'Isenye', proof pp. 5-6, ex. (7); 'Comparing the systems and conclusions', proof pp. 10-11 (journal ~368-369), ex. (16)
1193.prule: No stress rule. Privative H vs. zero tone system (syllable = TBU). Nominal tone is lexical with the noun stem as domain and only two patterns: H on the stem-initial syllable, or H multiply linked to all stem syllables (prefixes toneless); obligatory (+Oblig(H)) but not culminative (-Culm(H)), left-aligned to the stem, not weight-sensitive in nouns. Verbs may be toneless; verbal melodic (inflectional) tones are edge-aligned and weight-sensitive (Aunio 2013). Author explicitly tests and rejects a penultimate-stress reading: mono- and trisyllabic stems (final H, antepenultimate H) do not fit it.
1193.quote: Isenye has only two tonal patterns, namely a H tone on the first syllable of the stem or a H tone linked to all syllables of the stem (7). The domain of the lexical tone is the nominal stem; noun class prefixes are toneless. Isenye nouns satisfies the stress-related criterion of obligatoriness (every word has at least one syllable with the highest prominence) but not culminativity, since multiply linked H (‘all H’) tones are allowed. Both H tones are aligned with the left edge of the stem, which can be viewed as a metrical restriction (Downing 2004). ... With this rather restricted tonal syst…

Laine 2023 (fn. 18) gives the endonym Ishenyi: '"Isenye" is an alternative name for Ishenyi, and admittedly the…
1193.tone: Restricted ('two-type') Bantu tone system analysed with Hyman's stress diagnostics: Isenye nouns are [+Oblig(H), -Culm(H)]; the author treats pitch-accent as not a typological category and describes no stress. She raises, then qualifies, a possible drift toward Swahili-type penultimate stress (bisyllabic stems mostly stem-initial = penultimate H, but monosyllabic stems have final H and trisyllabic stems antepenultimate H, which 'does not match the pattern of penultimate stress'). evidence_works.work: Aunio, Robinson, Roth, Stegen & Walker 2019, The Mara languages (JE40) (The Bantu Languages, 2nd edn., Routledge: 501-532)
evidence_works.note: The chapter's statements on Isenye tone are two sentences in one paragraph of section 2.3, credited to Aunio 2015; the second reads 'In Isenye, there are only two tone types for all noun stems: either there is a H tone on the first syllable of the noun stem or all the stem syllables are H' (Helda final draft p. 10). It places this in family context: the Mara languages 'have previously been reported as accentual or "two type" languages with fairly reduced or non-existent lexical tonal contrasts (Bastin 2003)' but 'many have more than two lexical tonal contrasts' (p. 7); Nata and Isenye 'do not share the nominal tone system of Ikoma', Nata being 'a stress system in which every noun can have only one stressed syllable, realised as a H tone' (p. 10). Isenye is not one of the chapter's six target varieties ('viz. Ikizu, Ikoma, Kabwa, Ngoreme, Simbiti, and Zanaki', p. 2), so the verbal-tone claim 'All six languages lack lexical tonal contrast in the verb stem' (p. 10) does not cover Isenye; the row note's 'synthesis covering both nominal and verbal tone for Isenye' is not supported by the text.

evidence_works.work: Laine 2016, Isenjen kielen vokaalijärjestelmä [The vowel system of Isenye] (MA thesis, University of Helsinki: ii+72 pp.)
evidence_works.note: A vowel study, not a tone or stress study. Tone is explicitly left untreated: 'Myöskään isenjen toonijärjestelmää ei ole vielä kattavasti tutkittu enkä käsittele sitä tässä työssä' (the Isenye tone system has not yet been comprehensively studied and I do not treat it in this work; p. 2), and the two nominal tone types are restated from Aunio 2015 (p. 3), so on tone it only cites-for-stress. Its first-hand contribution is a length observation in section 4.2: 'Sen sijaan penultima, joka tyypillisesti saa bantukielissä paljon prominenssia, ei isenjessä välttämättä pidenny' (the penult, which in Bantu languages typically receives much prominence, does not necessarily lengthen in Isenye; p. 42), i.e. no penultimate lengthening of the kind that accompanies Bantu penultimate stress. Material: a 916-word SIL/UTB wordlist (266 verbs, the rest nouns) from one male speaker, each word recorded once (p. 32), analysed in Praat (p. 33); what was measured are formant frequencies for vowel quality, with duration measurements only 'preliminary' (phonemic vs conditioned length differing by 'some tens of milliseconds', p. 48). The penult statement is a transcription-level observation on that wordlist, not a stress experiment.

1195.prule: Penultimate stress is the normal pattern ('la sílaba tónica queda penúltima, como es normal'); stress stays penultimate even under apocope. Non-penult classes: agudas (final stress) are exemplified in sec. 1.5.2 (ahuel, ijquïn, ijcõn, nicpiá, nicpiáj, sejsÿ; likewise the demonstratives inïn 'este', inõn 'ese', sec. 8.1.1) and include every verb whose present ends in accented -iá / -á (third conjugation, sec. 4.1.1: motâliá 'se sienta'; group A, sec. 18.5: hueyá, tachá, quipiá), the vocatives in -u / -j (sec. 7.1: ¡Notáu!, Pêdrój, 'se acentúa la última sílaba'), plus 'contracted' preterite verb forms where the final syllable drops without stress shift (quiné', nictojtó'); esdrújulas/sobresdrújulas (antepenult and earlier) arise only when one or more enclitic particles are added, which never move the stress.

1196.tone: Lexical tone coexists with stress: JIPA follows Pickett's two/three-tone analysis organized into tone melodies and notes that Mock (1985, 1988, 'Pitch accent and stress in Isthmus Zapotec') recast the system as pitch accents, an analysis 'questioned in Yip 2002: 235-236'. Stress is described separately from tone and is cued by modal-vowel lengthening before lenis consonants, fortis-consonant lengthening after the stressed vowel, and a sharp fall of low tone in stressed syllables (its onset is slightly lower in unstressed pre-pause syllables); popular grammar sec. 3.4: 'cada sílaba tiene un tono particular'. Not coded tone or pitch accent because both primaries state a stress rule independent of tone (Cuadro 6 pair naga'/nagá' is tone-matched b.al).

tn.quote: The primary phonetic correlates of stress in Chajul Ixil are higher pitch and intensity, in which stressed syllables within a particular grouping are more prominent than the other syllables in that grouping. … Intonational phenomena include the marking of boundaries of declarative utterances. Intonational phrases consisting of normal declarative clauses are finalized with a falling boundary tone sequence that consists of a high tone followed by a low tone. The high tone always falls on the penultimate mora, while the low tone falls on the ultimate.
tn.cite: Adell, Eric James. 2019. The Phonetics, Phonology, and Morphology of Chajul Ixil (Mayan). PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Austin.
tn.locator: sec. 2.5.2 'Lexical stress', p. 189 and sec. 2.5.4 'Declarative boundary tones', p. 198
tn.note: No lexical tone is described: pitch (with intensity) is the correlate of word stress, and the only tones are intonational, a declarative boundary high on the penultimate mora followed by a final low.

1200.cfw: Adell's 2019 instrumental study of Chajul Ixil finds quantity-insensitive trochaic stress, root-initial for most speakers and penultimate for a minority and for Nebaj, and explains the final stress on long vowels reported by Ayres 1991 as a declarative boundary high tone on the penultimate mora, so the older weight-sensitive description is outweighed but only one modern source stands behind the new reading.

1201.prule: Stress accent (acento de intensidad), one per phonological word; by default on the FIRST SYLLABLE OF THE STEM (tema), prefixes unstressed, stable under affixation/cliticization; but position 'no es totalmente predecible': many words (especially nouns, also verbs) are deuterotonic (second stem syllable) and must be lexically listed; a few bases shift stress onto/before plural suffixes; polysyllabic applicatives/adpositions are always stressed on the second syllable (counting a person prefix); the intensive suffix /eh/ generally shifts stress rightward onto the syllable immediately preceding the suffix ([ꞌhwemik] 'muchacho joven' > [hweꞌmiki] 'muchacho muy joven'). Author treats stress as distinctive though no exact minimal pairs found (near-minimal pairs given).

1202.prule: Lexical accent system, stated for Chorote and illustrated specifically with Manjui (Forest Chorote): stress is contrastive; morphemes (roots and some suffixes, e.g. plural /-ís/, /-ájh/) are underlyingly accented or unaccented; the leftmost underlying accent in the word surfaces and all subsequent accents are deleted; if no morpheme carries an accent, default stress goes on the peninitial syllable (the only syllable in monosyllables). Iyo'awujwa'/Manjui are conservative and allow post-peninitial stress (e.g. Mj [ʔinʔlaˈhajh] 'one's words'), unlike Riverine Iyojwa'aja', which retracted it to the peninitial. Carol 2014 fn. 22 concurs in outline: montaraz facts 'similares', position not fully predictable, with many stems deuterotonic that are prototonic in Iyojwa'aja'.
